newsitem.title: USA: Secretary of State Christopher resigning -officials.
newsitem.headline: Secretary of State Christopher resigning -officials.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher has resigned but will remain in his post until after President Bill Clinton's inauguration in January, officials said on Wednesday.
Christopher discussed his plans with Clinton on Tuesday in Little Rock, Arkansas, Clinton's hometown, where his election night victory celebration was held.
Speaking to reporters aboard his Air Force One aircraft on his way back to Washington from Little Rock, Clinton did not specifically confirm Christopher's resignation but said:
"I had a warm conversation. We're very close and we have an unusual relationship. I've never known anybody quite like him. I think people have come to appreciate him more over time."
Officials said Christopher, who has a heavy schedule of commitments over the next two months, would continue in his post until Clinton is sworn in for a second term on January 20.

Christopher, who recently set a one-term record for secretaries of state by flying over 700,000 miles (a million km) in his job, is due to travel next week to a Middle East economic summit in Cairo and a meeting on Bosnia in Paris.

Two days after returning from that trip, he leaves for an important visit to China to try to advance a more stable relationship with a country seen as playing an increasingly key role into the 21st century.
It has been assumed for some time that Christopher would not serve a second term, even if Clinton were re-elected.
U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright and former Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell are considered leading candidates to succeed him.

But in the past 24 hours officials have increasingly indicated that Mitchell -- who has tried but so far failed to mediate peace in Northern Ireland -- has an edge after helping Clinton prepare for pre-election debates with Dole.
Mitchell would have more expertise in dealing with Congress but Albright has more hands-on foreign policy experience. She would be the first woman to serve in the top post if appointed.
Insiders have still not ruled out as possible candidates former Bosnia peacemaker Richard Holbrooke and former Vice President Walter Mondale, now ambassador to Japan.
Many officials believe Holbrooke could become U.N. ambassador if Albright moved up.
White House officials say Clinton wants to move quickly on a package of new cabinet appointments before he leaves for Asia next week.
Christopher, who recently turned 71, has weathered many diplomatic crises in nearly four years as top U.S. statesman.

During his first two years he endured withering criticism over America's policy on Bosnia, seen as weak and ambivalent, and offered to resign in late 1994. His post was discussed with General Colin Powell, ex-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, who turned it down.

Christopher stayed on and can now boast a number of achievements, including the 1995 Bosnia peace deal and several arms control accords, like the Comprehensive Test Ban treaty and a nuclear pact with North Korea.

But Christopher has failed to leave an unambiguous personal mark on the diplomatic successes of his tenure and he shares at least some blame for the failures, including a seriously troubled U.S. relationship with China.

He never established himself as a major presence, here or abroad. His steady, understated manner has made him an effective behind-the-scenes negotiator and a valued adviser to Clinton. But these qualities often let his lieutenants outshine him.
Christopher has wanted above all to cap his tenure with an Israel-Syrian treaty that would cement a truly historic and comprehensive peace in the Middle East.

But that goal became more elusive than ever with the election of a hardline government in Israel last spring and he has been left to focus on just trying to salvage already-signed agreements between Israel and Palestinians.
